chapter_en: Kil'ayim of Seeds and Kil'ayim of the Vineyard

sections.body_en:
We have been commanded not to sow two kinds of seeds together in a field in the Land of Israel, but rather each kind by itself, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes … you shall not sow your field with kil'ayim." Kil'ayim means a mixture. Included in the prohibition are kinds of grain, legumes and vegetables that are fit to be eaten. But kinds of plants that are intended for ornament or for medicine are not included in the prohibition. The prohibition of kil'ayim of seeds applies to annual kinds of plants, which are grain, legumes and vegetables, but there is no prohibition against sowing trees intermingled, and likewise there is no prohibition against sowing kinds of trees together with an annual kind. For even when the trees are intermingled, by virtue of their size each tree has its own distinct place. And the seeds between them also have a distinct place, since the trees grow upward and their roots branch out over a great distance, so that room is left for the annual kind to survive among them.

Also one who waters, or fertilizes, or weeds out thorns, or assists in some other way in the growth of the kil'ayim transgresses a Torah prohibition whose punishment is lashes. And even when the kil'ayim grew by themselves in his field, as long as he wants them, or it appears as though he wants them, he is obligated to uproot them, for it is forbidden to maintain kil'ayim in a field (Rambam, Hilkhot Kil'ayim 1:1-3).

If one transgressed and deliberately sowed kil'ayim, the produce is permitted to be eaten, because the prohibition is to sow and grow kil'ayim, but there is no prohibition against eating what grows from them (Rambam, ibid. 1:7). Only in the case of kil'ayim of the vineyard is the produce forbidden to be eaten.

The prohibition of kil'ayim of seeds applies in the Land of Israel, and even in land that belongs to a gentile it is forbidden for a Jew to sow kil'ayim. But outside the Land a Jew is permitted to sow kil'ayim, since the prohibition is stated regarding "your field," and only the Land of Israel is considered "your field." Even the Sages did not prohibit kil'ayim of seeds outside the Land; they prohibited only kil'ayim of the vineyard outside the Land, because of their extra severity, as they are forbidden to be eaten and to derive benefit from (above, 4:4).

Also in a flowerpot in the Land of Israel it is forbidden to sow two kinds together, except that if the pot has a hole, it is considered attached to the ground and the prohibition is from the Torah, and if it has no hole, it is detached from the ground and the prohibition is rabbinic.1

notes_en.en:
One who performs an action in order to sow the kil'ayim or to make them grow is punished with lashes; and if they came up by themselves and he wants them, then as long as he has not uprooted them he transgresses a Torah prohibition but does not receive lashes, since it involves no action (Yerushalmi Kil'ayim 8:1, and so wrote the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim and most of the Aḥaronim; some say it is rabbinically forbidden – the Gra and the Ḥazon Ish). According to most poskim, the Torah prohibition is in sowing them "be-mapolet yad," meaning sowing the two seeds together [with one cast of the hand]. Included in this is also performing an action to make them grow together, such as covering with soil, watering, fertilizing and weeding out wild grasses (Tosafot, Rash, the Gra and others). Some say that also one who sows one kind beside a second kind, without tending to both of them together, transgresses a Torah prohibition (Kaftor Va-feraḥ and Mishna Rishona). In our times as well, the prohibition of kil'ayim is from the Torah, and it applies within the borders settled by those who came up from Egypt (below 12:2, note 2).
Animal fodder together with human food is kil'ayim, but all kinds of animal fodder are considered as one kind, so that mixing them does not constitute kil'ayim (Kesef Mishneh, Taz and others). And some say that there is no prohibition of kil'ayim with animal fodder, even together with human food (Radbaz; Mishpat Kohen 26). Some say that any plant, when a whole field of it is grown, such as cotton, even though it is not intended for human food, is subject to the prohibition of kil'ayim with human food (Mabit). Some say that even inside a house the prohibition of kil'ayim is from the Torah (Yeshu'ot Malko 1:1; Ḥazon Ish), and some say it is rabbinic (Mishpat Kohen 49; Eretz Ḥemda pp. 21-22). And it seems that in a greenhouse the prohibition is from the Torah, since that is the normal way of growing them.

sections.title_en: Mar'it Ayin in Kil'ayim of Seeds
sections.body_en:
The Torah prohibition of kil'ayim applies when a person sows, or willingly maintains, two kinds together, but when they grew in his field without his wanting them, there is no prohibition. However, the Sages forbade the owner of the field to maintain kil'ayim in his field even when he is not interested in them, because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers), for since the field is open to all, passersby will think that the owner of the field does not care about keeping the mitzvot, and the result will be that the name of Heaven is desecrated. Therefore, one who wishes to sow his field with wheat and sees that barley seeds have become mixed in among his wheat seeds, as long as the barley does not amount to a quantity capable of producing one twenty-fourth of the field (1/24 – 4.16%), may sow the field with the seeds he has, because with such a small quantity there is no concern of mar'it ayin, for all who see it understand that the barley is growing there against his will. And although it is forbidden to sow even a single barley grain in a wheat field, and if he deliberately mixed a single barley grain among the wheat, it is forbidden for him to sow the wheat without removing the barley grain; nevertheless, when he does not want the barley that became mixed into the wheat and it is troublesome for him to remove it, as long as it does not amount to 1/24, there is no concern of mar'it ayin and he is permitted to sow it in the field. And if there is enough of it to produce 1/24 of the field, he must reduce the barley or add more wheat until he is certain that the barley will produce less than 1/24 of the field. Likewise, one who sows his field with one kind and sees that another kind has grown along with it: if he is interested in the second kind, he must uproot all of it, since it is kil'ayim. But if he is not interested in it, if its share is less than 1/24 of the field, he need not reduce it, and if its share is 1/24, he must reduce it until it is less than 1/24.2

Because of the importance of the mitzva and the gravity of the desecration of God's name caused by those who transgress it, every year on Rosh Ḥodesh Adar, at the time when grain and vegetables begin to sprout in the fields, the messengers of the beit din would rouse Israel to beware of kil'ayim (Mishna Shekalim 1:1). On the fifteenth of Adar the messengers of the beit din would go out to inspect the fields; if they found kil'ayim, they would uproot the lesser kind and throw it before the animals of the owner of the field. And the owners of the fields were happy with two joys: one, that their fields had been weeded, and one, that their animals had been fed; and they would not bother to uproot the kil'ayim themselves. So it was instituted that the messengers would uproot the kil'ayim and throw them onto the roads, for the benefit of animals in general. And still the owners of the fields were happy that their fields had been weeded, and they would not bother to uproot the kil'ayim. So it was instituted that the messengers of the beit din would declare ownerless (hefker) everything growing in fields in which they found kil'ayim, and from then on the owners of the fields were careful about kil'ayim (Mo'ed Katan 6b). It should be noted that from the moment the representatives of the beit din declared the kil'ayim ownerless, the owner of the field no longer transgresses a prohibition through them, for there is no prohibition of kil'ayim with ownerless property.

notes_en.en: Mishna Kil'ayim 2:1; Rambam, Hilkhot Kil'ayim 2:1-10. Some say that by Torah law the minority is nullified in the majority, since the owner of the field does not want it to exist, but the Sages forbade sowing or maintaining the minority when it amounts to 1/24 because of mar'it ayin, lest people think he mixed them deliberately; but when they are less than 1/24, there is no concern of mar'it ayin, because it is not customary to deliberately mix in less than 1/24, and on the contrary, it is common for such a small quantity to get mixed in unintentionally (Rash, Rosh, Rav Ovadia of Bartenura, Rash Sirilio). And some say that even without his wanting it, if the minority amounts to 1/24, the kil'ayim are forbidden by Torah law, because the Torah prohibition depends on how it appears, and it appears that he wants kil'ayim in his field (the Rambam according to most of his commentators). And we do not say that the minority is nullified in the majority, because only with an opposing kind, such as a forbidden substance in a permitted one, is the minority nullified, whereas here, where both kinds are permitted, the minority is not nullified in the majority. In addition, when the minority is noticeable it is not nullified. However, since it is almost impossible to ensure that no seed whatsoever gets mixed into another seed, and the Torah was not given to the ministering angels, the Sages learned that the intention of the Torah is that as long as there is no intention to sow kil'ayim, the matter is forbidden by Torah law only when a noticeable quantity of 1/24, which involves mar'it ayin, became mixed in (Responsa Rashba 1:259). For buyers are particular about such a quantity (Bava Batra 94a). When it is evident to all that he does not want the second kind to remain, for example when it is known to be harmful, he need not reduce it even when it is 1/24.

sections.title_en: The Required Distances in Kil'ayim of Seeds
sections.body_en:
The basic rule in the laws of kil'ayim of seeds is that if the two kinds appear separate from one another, it is permitted, and if they appear mixed, it is forbidden. The larger the field, the greater the distance required, so that the separation between them will be evident. The law likewise depends on the abundance of the leaves, their size and their length: with grain, whose stalks are tall, a large separation is required, and with vegetables a small separation, except for vegetables whose leaves are especially large.

Vegetables: By Torah law, the distance between one vegetable and another is one tefaḥ (about 8 cm), and the Sages added a safeguard and required a distance of a tefaḥ and a half (about 12 cm). When the two kinds were distanced properly, and the branches grew until they were touching one another, since there is a gap of a tefaḥ and a half between the stalks that come out of the ground, there is no prohibition of kil'ayim. This is except for a few kinds of vegetables such as gourds, whose leaves are especially large and tend to become entangled in the kind next to them, where one must take care that the leaves of the two kinds do not reach one another. All this concerns beds in a garden, but in the case of two fields of vegetables, they must be separated by a square of an ama by an ama (an ama is about half a meter), and along the rest of the border between the fields it is proper to keep a distance of a tefaḥ.3

Grain: Since grain is usually sown over large areas, the distance required between kinds is greater. By Torah law the distance is an ama, and the Sages added a safeguard and determined that an ama suffices only when dealing with small plots whose width is less than an ama; but if the grain was sown in medium-sized plots (meishar) whose width is at least an ama, they must be separated by a square of two amot by two amot (about a meter by a meter), which then narrows diagonally [diagram] until only a minimal amount remains between the fields. And if the grain was sown, as is customary, in large fields, they must be separated by a square of about five meters by five meters (beit rova), and along the rest of the area it is proper to leave a gap of an ama along the length of the two fields.4

Regarding legumes, there is a dispute whether their law is like grain or like vegetables, and because of the doubt, in any size of field there must be an ama between the two crops.5 When one sows grain next to vegetables or legumes, or vegetables next to legumes, the laws are complex and depend on the size of the field, but in any case they are no more stringent than for grain.

If there was a partition ten tefaḥim high (about 80 cm) between the two fields, even a partition of reeds with no more than three tefaḥim between one reed and the next, there is no longer any need to separate the fields, for the partition separates them. And even if it is known that beneath the ground the roots of the two kinds are intertwined with one another, as long as the separation between them is evident by means of a partition, there is no prohibition of kil'ayim. Likewise, if there was a path four amot wide (1.84 meters) between the fields, or a plowed strip of that width, there is no need for the separation of the large square (five meters by five meters).

notes_en.en:
According to the opinion of most Rishonim and Aḥaronim, by Torah law a tefaḥ suffices to separate vegetables, and rabbinically a tefaḥ and a half. This is the opinion of: Rabbenu Ḥananel, Rambam, Rash, Rosh, Rav Ovadia of Bartenura, Kaftor Va-feraḥ and SA 297:34, and others. (Some say that rabbinically three tefaḥim are required – Rashi, Rabbenu Tam and Ritva. Some say six tefaḥim – the Gra. And some say that even rabbinically a tefaḥ suffices – the Ge'onim, Rav Sa'adia Gaon.) A bed for which a distance of a tefaḥ and a half suffices is up to an ama long (six tefaḥim, about half a meter); a field, which requires a distance of a square ama, is according to the Ḥazon Ish an area of a beit rova, about 22 square meters (10.2 amot by 10.2 amot), and according to Rav Yisraeli a beit tish'a kabin – about 780 square meters. When the growing area is larger than a bed and smaller than a field, according to the Ḥazon Ish a separation of a tefaḥ and a half is required, or a furrow a tefaḥ deep and a tefaḥ wide, and according to Rav Yisraeli a furrow is always required (according to the Rash along the entire area, and according to the Rambam along six tefaḥim, after which a gap of a tefaḥ suffices).
The precise measures: a tefaḥ is 7.6 cm; an ama – six tefaḥim – 45.6 cm; a beit rova – ten and a fifth amot by ten and a fifth amot – 4.65 meters by 4.65 meters (Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 2, note 1). SA 296:68 explains that with kil'ayim the measures must be expanded to a generous ("soḥek") tefaḥ and ama. And we have added rounding upward: the tefaḥ to 8 cm, as the measure of Rav Ḥayim Na'eh, and the ama to half a meter.

Field: As we learned in the previous note regarding vegetables, a field according to the Ḥazon Ish is about 22 square meters, and according to Rav Yisraeli about 780 square meters, and so it seems. It is explained in the Yerushalmi (Kil'ayim 2:4) regarding a meishar, that is, a small grain field whose width is more than an ama, that the measure of the gap between meisharim is a square of two amot by two amot, "and it narrows progressively, even to the slightest amount." There is a dispute whether also regarding the gap between vegetable fields, which is an ama by an ama, and between grain fields, which is a beit rova (a square of about ten amot), it must narrow progressively along a diagonal down to the slightest amount. According to the Ḥazon Ish (Kil'ayim 6:1, 1), after the square it must narrow progressively along a diagonal line, and beyond that there is no need to separate the kinds. According to Tiferet Yisrael (Kil'ayim 2:73), immediately after the end of the square one may place the two kinds adjacent to each other. And according to my teacher Rav Yisraeli this is the essential law, but it is proper to maintain a distance of a tefaḥ between kinds of vegetables and of an ama between kinds of grain along the entire field, as the measure required by Torah law. And so it seems in practice, in keeping with the main principle of kil'ayim of seeds, that one must separate between the kinds.

According to my teacher Rav Yisraeli, the law of legumes is like that of vegetables; however, even in the small measures of a garden bed a furrow is required between them, and a tefaḥ and a half does not suffice (Eretz Ḥemda pp. 85, 144-149). According to the Ḥazon Ish, legumes have the law of grain (6:2; 8:2). And because of the doubt, insofar as it concerns a doubt in Torah law one must be stringent, so that even in small areas a separation of an ama is required; however, even if large fields of them are sown, one may suffice with an ama, which is obligatory by Torah law, and one need not require the separation that the Sages added, for a doubt in rabbinic law is resolved leniently (Hilkhot Ha-aretz of Makhon Ha-Torah Ve-ha'aretz, Kil'ayim 5:14).

sections.title_en: Kil'ayim of the Vineyard: The Foundations of the Mitzva
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to sow grain or vegetables beside grapevines, or to plant a vine beside grain or vegetables, and if one did so, both become forbidden to be eaten and to derive benefit from, as it is stated (Devarim 22:9): "You shall not sow your vineyard with kil'ayim, lest the full produce of the seed that you sow and the yield of the vineyard become consecrated (tikdash)." Tikdash means it becomes defiled and forbidden for benefit; "the full produce of the seed that you sow" – the grain or the vegetables; and "the yield of the vineyard" – these are the grapes. Even the straw of the grain and the wood of the vines become forbidden for benefit, and it is a mitzva to burn them or destroy them in some other way so that people will not stumble with them (above 2, note 3). And it is forbidden to fire an oven for heating or a stove for cooking with them while burning them, because it is forbidden to derive benefit from them (Rambam, Hilkhot Kil'ayim 5:7). The prohibition of kil'ayim of the vineyard applies by Torah law in the Land of Israel, and rabbinically also outside the Land (below, 4).

The Torah prohibition of kil'ayim applies to a vine together with the five species of grain, or legumes, or vegetables. But not to kinds of trees, even if they are small, for whenever their blessing is Ha-etz, they are not subject to the prohibition of kil'ayim of the vineyard. On the other hand, any plant whose blessing is Ha-adama is forbidden as kil'ayim of the vineyard (above 2:8).

Also spices over which one does not recite Ha-adama, because they are not eaten on their own (Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 8:14), as long as they are kinds of plants that, were they eaten on their own, their blessing would be Ha-adama, are included in the prohibition of kil'ayim of the vineyard.

The Sages further forbade also kinds of grasses and vegetables that are usually fed to animals. But kinds of plants that are not usually fed even to animals are not included in the prohibition (Levush 296:2).

Regarding plants intended for their fragrance, some forbid them rabbinically and some permit them. In practice, ideally it is good to be stringent, and one who wishes to be lenient may do so. However, with plants intended for ornament there is no prohibition. Therefore, it is permitted to plant beneath a vine grass and flowers that are not usually fed to animals, even if they have a medicinal use.1

[Video]

notes_en.en:
Regarding the punishment of lashes, the Amoraim disagreed (Yerushalmi Kil'ayim 8:1): according to Rabbi Yonatan, one who sows one kind of grain or vegetable in a vineyard receives lashes. And according to Rabbi Yoshiya, since it is stated (Devarim 22:9): "You shall not sow your vineyard with kil'ayim," it refers to seeds that even without the vineyard are kil'ayim. In the Bavli (Berakhot 22a; Kiddushin 39a) only the opinion of Rabbi Yoshiya is cited, that one who sows wheat and barley together with a grape pip from which a vine will grow, or even covers them with soil, receives lashes. The meaning is that he receives lashes twice, once for kil'ayim of seeds and once for kil'ayim of the vineyard. And so ruled the Rambam (Hilkhot Kil'ayim 5:1-2); however, he ruled that there is a Torah prohibition against sowing one kind of grain or vegetable near a vine, or a vine near grain or vegetables, except that one does not receive lashes for this, and what grows from this is forbidden by Torah law, and one who eats a kezayit of it receives lashes (Hilkhot Kil'ayim 5:7; Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 10:6). This is also the opinion of the Yere'im, and the Radbaz there. According to the Ramban and the Ran, sowing two kinds near a planted vine is forbidden by Torah law, but one kind is permitted. According to the Ramah and the Sefer Ha-ḥinukh, one kind is rabbinically forbidden. And according to Rabbenu Tam and the Ri, once the vine is planted it is permitted to sow beside it even two kinds or more, because the words of Rabbi Yoshiya are not only about the punishment of lashes but also about the prohibition itself, that only in sowing two kinds together with a grape pip is there a prohibition of kil'ayim. The halakha follows the Rambam, as ruled in SA 296:3; Levush; and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 296:13.
All kinds of grain, legumes and vegetables intended for human food are forbidden in a vineyard by Torah law, and animal fodder is forbidden rabbinically. As explained in the Mishna (Kil'ayim 5:8), one who maintains in a vineyard thorns that are usually fed to animals has rendered the vineyard forbidden, but the iris, the ivy and the "king's lily," which are not usually fed to animals, are not kil'ayim in a vineyard. So summarized the Levush (YD 296:2), and so one can understand from the Rambam (Hilkhot Kil'ayim 5:3, 6, 19), and so wrote the Kesef Mishneh (5:3). And some say that only grain, hemp and arum are forbidden in a vineyard by Torah law, since only these kinds are mentioned in the Talmud: grain because of its importance, and hemp and arum because of their resemblance to the vine, or because they grow for three years together with the vine. But other kinds of legumes and vegetables that are eaten by people or animals are forbidden rabbinically (Rabbenu Tam; Tosafot Yevamot 83a, s.v. "Rabbi Yosei"; Semag; Rashba). This approach branches out into many approaches, such as, for example, those who hold that since legumes resemble grain, their law is like grain, whose prohibition is from the Torah (Maharit Tzahalon according to the Rambam, and similarly in the work attributed to the Rashba, Menaḥot 15b). Since the prohibition applies to vegetables intended for food, this also includes vegetables intended for seasoning.
Regarding plants whose blessing is Borei Isvei Besamim (fragrant herbs), there is a dispute: some permit (Ḥazon Ish, Kil'ayim 1:14; Mishpetei Eretz 2:1). And one can add the opinion of Rabbenu Tam and the Ri, that there is no prohibition at all unless there are two kinds there with a grape pip sown together. And if only one kind is planted beside the vine, then even according to the Ramban and the Ran there is no prohibition. On the other hand, many poskim imply that it is rabbinically forbidden, and so wrote SA YD 108:7 (see Kedushat Ha-aretz 5:7). Regarding ornamental plants, such as flowers and grass, some are rabbinically stringent since they are fit for animals (Rav Eliyahu), and according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim it is permitted.

sections.body_en:
Kil'ayim of the vineyard are forbidden also to maintain (Mishna Kil'ayim 8:1). That is, even one who did not sow grain in his vineyard, if even a single stalk of grain grew in it, he must hurry to destroy it, for it is forbidden to maintain kil'ayim in a vineyard. However, there is a difference between one who sows and one who maintains. For one who sows a stalk of grain in his vineyard, immediately when it takes root, the stalk and the vines around it become forbidden for benefit. But one who finds a stalk of grain that grew in his vineyard – only after it grows an additional one two-hundredth will the prohibition of benefit take effect on it and on the vines. However, ideally it is a mitzva for him to hurry and destroy it immediately, because even one who is negligent and maintains them for a single moment transgresses a prohibition (Mishna ibid. 5:6; Pesaḥim 25a; Rambam 5:21-22; 6:1).2

And when do the vines become forbidden for benefit? When the grapes on them are discernible and are in their stages of growth and ripening, that is, from the time they reach the stage of boser (unripe grapes), meaning their shape is discernible and their size is at least that of a "white bean," until they are fully ripe. But if there are no grapes in the vineyard, or they have not yet reached the size of a "white bean," or they have already fully ripened, the vines do not become forbidden for benefit because of the grain or vegetables that grew next to them, even though the grain and the vegetables do become forbidden.

And when does the grain become forbidden? From the time it takes root in the ground until the grain is fully ripe. And if, after the grain has finished ripening, someone trained over it a vine with grapes at the stage at which they become forbidden, the whole vine becomes forbidden, but the grain does not become forbidden (Mishna Kil'ayim 7:7).3

If the wind blew and bent one's vine over his grain, he must hurry to separate them immediately, and if there is a concern that they will become mixed again, he must cut the branches of the vine or erect a fence that will prevent them from becoming mixed again. And if he was negligent and they remained mixed, and one of them grew by one two-hundredth, they become forbidden. But if, due to circumstances beyond his control, he was unable to separate them by then, they do not become forbidden (Mishna 7:7, Rivmatz and Rash there; Rambam 5:11, Kesef Mishneh and Mahari Korkos).

A person cannot render forbidden something that is not his. Therefore, if one spreads his vine over his fellow's grain, his vine becomes forbidden and his fellow's grain is permitted. If he spread his fellow's vine over his own grain, his grain becomes forbidden and his fellow's vine is permitted. If he spread his fellow's vine over another fellow's grain, both are permitted. However, as soon as the owner of the vine or the grain learns of the kil'ayim, he must hurry to separate them, and if he was negligent until one of them grew an additional one two-hundredth, his share too becomes forbidden. In any case, for the one who mixed the kil'ayim with his own hands, even what is not his becomes forbidden. Not only that, but if a person passed by his fellow's vineyard and saw that stalks of grain had come up in it, and he knows that his fellow agrees to this, he is obligated to uproot them. Likewise, a worker who works there is obligated to uproot the kil'ayim. And if they did not do so, the vine and the grain that grew there are forbidden to them for benefit. But for the owner of the vineyard there is no prohibition, for only from the time he learns of the kil'ayim must he hurry to uproot the stalks, and only if he was negligent and they continued to grow by one two-hundredth do they become forbidden to him and to all of Israel (Mishna Kil'ayim 7:4; Rambam, Hilkhot Kil'ayim 5:8-9, 21; Taz 296:3).

[Video]

notes_en.en:
Our master Rav Kook explained (Mishpat Kohen 24) according to the Rambam that the prohibition upon an increase of one two-hundredth is from the Torah, for the Torah, which forbade growing kil'ayim, gave the Sages the authority to determine what the measure of growth is, and they determined that it is one two-hundredth. So too wrote the Yere'im 389, and so it is implied by the Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 549. And some say that by Torah law the prohibition applies when the majority of the growth occurred as kil'ayim, and the Sages forbade it at one two-hundredth (Kiryat Sefer, Kil'ayim ch. 5; Minḥat Ḥinukh there; Derekh Emuna 5:146). In any case, it seems that if the owner of the vineyard is not interested in the kil'ayim, the prohibition is rabbinic, because of mar'it ayin, as with kil'ayim of seeds above 4:2, at less than 1/24 (Derekh Emuna 5:141). In the past, destroying grain or vegetables that came up in a vineyard was done by uprooting them, and in my humble opinion, nowadays it is possible to destroy them also by spraying with herbicides, and even though several days will pass until they die, since they are in the process of being destroyed, there is no prohibition involved.
Sometimes wild plants grow in a vineyard, including wild stalks of grain, and ideally it is good to eliminate them by mowing or by spraying once, for by doing so he will eliminate them and show that he is not interested in them if they grow back. However, by strict law this is not necessary, since these are plants that at most are considered animal fodder, whose prohibition is rabbinic, and the owner of the vineyard is not interested in them. And if he wants grasses to grow in his vineyard in order to loosen and improve the soil, and therefore does not want to mow or spray them, he is not obligated to do so, since these grasses are not intended for animal fodder, and on the contrary, he maintains them for a different purpose, and only what is intended for animal fodder is rabbinically forbidden.

The law is the same for legumes; however, with vegetables, even after the produce has finished ripening, the vegetable sometimes grows additional produce, and therefore only after its last produce finishes ripening will it not become forbidden.
According to the Rash and the Rosh (in their commentary on Mishna Kil'ayim 7:7), the prohibition of benefit from the grain and from the vines is not interdependent, and whatever has reached the stage at which it becomes forbidden, whether grain or vine, is forbidden by Torah law. And according to the Rambam (5:14), by Torah law their prohibition is interdependent, and therefore only when both are at the stage at which they become forbidden is their prohibition from the Torah. However, rabbinically, even where only one of them has reached the stage of prohibition, the kind that reached the stage of prohibition becomes forbidden. So wrote the Aḥaronim (Levush 296:9-10, Tiferet Yisrael, Sha'arei Tzedek).
One who transgresses and sows grain or vegetables in a vineyard – from the time the grain and vegetables take root, they become forbidden. And if he passed through a vineyard with a perforated flowerpot containing grain or vegetables, or if they came up by themselves in the vineyard, according to the Rambam (5:23), here too from the time they grew an additional one two-hundredth they become forbidden. And according to the Rash and the Rosh (Mishna Kil'ayim 7:7; 8), they become forbidden through an increase of one two-hundredth only from the time they reached a third [of their growth]. Since the dispute concerns Torah law, one must be stringent. And so wrote SA 296:16-17, Levush, Sha'arei Tzedek, and Arukh Ha-shulḥan 29.

sections.title_en: The Measure of the Prohibited Distance
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of kil'ayim is that kinds of grain and vegetables should not be mixed with the vines, and the Torah gave the Sages the authority to determine, according to their judgment, what is considered mixed and what is not, and what they determine is considered part of the Torah's mitzva. There are three main situations of mixing in the laws of kil'ayim of the vineyard, and we will arrange them according to their severity: a) near a single vine; b) near a vineyard; c) inside a vineyard.

A single vine: One who wishes to sow grain or vegetables near a single vine must keep a distance of six generous tefaḥim (about 47 cm) from it, which is the measure required for the vine's bed and the work around it. Likewise, grain or vegetables may not grow beneath the vine's branches, for if a stalk of grain grew beneath one of the branches, or the leaves or the clusters growing from it, even if it is a hundred amot away from the base of the vine, and he was negligent and did not uproot it, the stalk and the entire vine become forbidden for benefit (as explained in halakha 2). And if there was doubt whether the stalk is beneath it, the location of the stalk is measured with a plumb line. Since the branches of a vine extend over great distances, one must take care that along their entire length no grain or vegetables grow beneath them.

It is customary to train the vine on poles or ropes, and the Sages decreed that also beneath the continuation of the pole or rope that the branch has not yet reached, grain or vegetables should not grow, because the branch will eventually extend there. However, after the fact, as long as the grain or the vegetables were not actually beneath the vine itself, they do not become forbidden (Rambam, Hilkhot Kil'ayim 6:11-12, 15).

A vineyard is a planting of vines planted precisely according to the accepted method of cultivation. Since a vineyard has importance, anyone who sows grain or vegetables within four amot of it appears to be mixing them into the vineyard and transgresses the prohibition of kil'ayim. The measure was set at four amot (about 188 cm) because that is the measure that was needed in the past for working the vineyard, for plowing around the vineyard was done with oxen, and at the time of the grape harvest they would transport the grapes from the vineyard to the market in wagons, and these four amot were needed for the oxen and the wagons.

For the vines to be considered a "vineyard," there must be at least two rows of vines, one opposite the other, with three vines in each row [diagram], or five vines arranged as "two opposite two and one extending as a tail," according to the Rambam [diagram] and according to the Rash [diagram]. If the vines are not in a straight row, even if there are many of them there, their law is that of a single vine.4

One who sows grain or vegetables within four amot of a vineyard renders forbidden from the vineyard the measure of a small vineyard, that is, the shape of a vineyard of the five vines closest to the kil'ayim. And if there were additional vines within four amot of the kil'ayim in every direction, they too become forbidden. It is further important to note that if a branch extended beyond the four amot of the vineyard, one must be careful with it as with a single vine, that is, that no grain or vegetables grow beneath it; and if they grew, that vine and everything growing beneath it become forbidden.

An aris (trellised row of vines) is considered like a vineyard. An aris is at least five vines planted in a straight row and trained on poles or wires so that they receive more sun and air and produce more abundant and better grapes. If the kil'ayim are within four amot of an aris, whether on the side of the vines' bases or on the side of the poles on which the vines are trained, the five vines opposite the kil'ayim become forbidden.

A fence ten tefaḥim high (about 80 cm) separates between the vineyard and the field, and it is permitted to sow grain and vegetables on the other side of the fence without any distance (Rambam 7:15). And although the roots of the vine reach beneath the grain, since the prohibition of kil'ayim is that they should not appear mixed, by means of the fence they do not appear mixed.

Inside the vineyard: If one sowed kil'ayim inside the vineyard, or they grew by themselves and he was negligent and did not uproot them, the mixing is more evident, and therefore its laws are much more severe, for we go by the absorption of the roots, which extend up to sixteen amot in every direction, and in addition to that another four amot. Thus, every vine that is less than twenty amot from the kil'ayim becomes forbidden for benefit (Rambam 6:1-2).

notes_en.en:
We must say that the Torah intended that the Sages determine the parameters of the prohibition, for the measure of distancing four amot from a vineyard, with the status of a Torah prohibition, was determined by the Sages, because the work of the vineyard, which includes plowing with cattle and a plow, as well as transporting the produce by wagon, requires four amot. However, the additional stringency regarding grain that grew inside the vineyard or in the meḥol ha-kerem (the open perimeter of the vineyard) is rabbinic. Regarding a single vine, it is explained in the Sifrei (Ki Tetze 230), Ramban and Ran, that distancing six tefaḥim from a single vine is from the Torah. That is, the measure that the Sages set for working a single vine is binding by Torah law. In contrast, several Rishonim imply that the prohibition of kil'ayim applies only to an actual vineyard, and the law of distancing from a single vine is entirely rabbinic (She'iltot; Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 548). And see the Harḥavot. All the measures of kil'ayim are in generous tefaḥim, as explained in SA 296:68. It is explained in the Harḥavot to Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 2:1:11, that we follow the opinion of the Rashba cited in Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 363:60, that the addition of a generous tefaḥ is about 1/48. So the measure of an ama, which is six tefaḥim (45.6 cm), comes out in practice to 46.55 cm, and we rounded it to 47 cm. And for four amot we rounded to 188 cm.
The Sages said that the distance between the rows of vines in a vineyard is between four amot and eight amot, and it is implied by the Rambam that this is also the case between one vine and the next within the same row. Nowadays it is customary that the distance between rows of vines is a little over four amot, but between one vine and the next about three amot. And it seems that since this is the optimal form of cultivation today, it is considered a vineyard. My teacher Rav Yisraeli wrote similarly, and he further added that according to the Rosh, even in the past there was no impediment to planting the vines within a row less than four amot apart (Eretz Ḥemda vol. 2, 7:1-3).

sections.title_en: Outside the Land and Kil'ayim of Gentiles
sections.body_en:
The Torah prohibition of kil'ayim of seeds and kil'ayim of the vineyard applies only in the Land, for it is stated regarding kil'ayim of seeds (Vayikra 19:19): "You shall keep My statutes … you shall not sow your field with kil'ayim …," and likewise it is stated regarding kil'ayim of the vineyard (Devarim 22:9): "You shall not sow your vineyard with kil'ayim," and the "field" and "vineyard" of Israel are in the Land of Israel. However, since the prohibition of kil'ayim of the vineyard is especially severe, in that the produce growing in it is forbidden to be eaten and for benefit, the Sages were stringent and enacted that it is forbidden also outside the Land. However, they determined that the prohibition outside the Land applies only to what all opinions agree is forbidden in the Land of Israel by Torah law, both in sowing and in benefit (Kiddushin 39a).

Therefore, there is no prohibition of kil'ayim outside the Land except for one who sows at one time a grape pip together with two other kinds of seeds that are kil'ayim with each other, such as two kinds of grain, or two kinds of vegetables, or a kind of vegetable and a kind of grain. And although in the Land of Israel the Torah prohibition of kil'ayim applies even to one who sows a single stalk of grain near a vine, and one who deliberately eats of what grows there is punished with lashes, since even in the Land of Israel one who sows kil'ayim receives lashes only if he sowed a grape pip with two kinds of seeds that are kil'ayim with each other, the prohibition of sowing kil'ayim outside the Land, and of benefiting from them, likewise applies only in this manner. But it is permitted to sow grain in one's vineyard outside the Land, and to eat of what grows there (Rema YD 296:69).5

Even though a gentile is permitted to sow kil'ayim in his vineyard in the Land of Israel, it is forbidden for a Jew to tell a gentile to sow kil'ayim in the Land of Israel (Rambam 8:13). Likewise, it is forbidden by Torah law to derive benefit from grapes, grain and vegetables that grew in a gentile's vineyard (Tosafot Kiddushin 36b, s.v. "kol," and Rosh). Therefore, it is forbidden to buy grapes or vegetables from gentiles near their vineyards, since there is a doubt whether perhaps they grew them in a prohibited manner; and if one transgressed and bought them, it is forbidden to derive benefit from the produce, for since the doubt arose near their fixed location, the produce is forbidden to be eaten and for benefit. But one who buys, in the market or in stores, grapes or vegetables that gentiles grew – since the doubt arose after they separated from their fixed location, we follow the majority, and the produce is permitted to be eaten. This law applies after the fact, when one has already bought produce and does not know its status, or for one who is in a place where there are no stores with a kashrut certificate and in order to reach such a store he would have to go to great trouble. But if there is a store there with a kashrut certificate, he must remove himself from the doubt and buy there. And even when the concern of prohibition is very remote, when possible one is obligated to remove oneself from the doubt. In addition, it is a mitzva to strengthen those who are meticulous about kashrut. Moreover, when there is a kashrut certificate, terumot and ma'asrot are also separated properly (as explained above 2:11).6

[Video]

notes_en.en: As we learned in note 1, there is a dispute regarding the obligation of lashes for one who sows in the Land, and the halakha was ruled in the Rambam according to the opinion of Rabbi Yoshiya, that only one who sows a grape pip and two kinds of seeds together receives lashes twice. And regarding outside the Land, the Sages said (Berakhot 22a; Kiddushin 39a) that the custom follows his opinion. Indeed, according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Kil'ayim 8:13-14), there is indeed no prohibition outside the Land to sow grain or vegetables in a vineyard, but what grows there is forbidden for benefit; and his reasoning is that just as what grows in this manner is forbidden for benefit by Torah law in the Land of Israel, so the Sages decreed regarding it outside the Land. However, according to the Rosh, Ra'avad and Terumat Ha-deshen 194, whatever is not forbidden to sow outside the Land is also not forbidden for benefit. And so ruled the Rema YD 296:69. And since the dispute concerns rabbinic law, the halakha follows the lenient opinion. And according to the Rosh, the Rambam also agrees with this, and only when one bought a vineyard containing vegetables is the Rambam concerned that perhaps they were sown together [with a grape pip], and therefore he forbade them.

The poskim permitted buying grapes and cucumbers from gentiles, even though there is a concern that they were grown in violation of the prohibition of kil'ayim, since most of them are not grown in a prohibited manner, and since the doubt arose after the produce had already separated from the gentile's field, the rule applies to them: "Whatever separates, separates from the majority." They further added various doubts and permitted on the basis of a double doubt (sefek sefeka), for in addition to the ordinary doubt, that perhaps these grapes and vegetables did not grow in a prohibited manner, perhaps the halakha follows Rabbi Yoshiya, as Rabbenu Tam and the Ri explained him (above, note 1), that as long as they were not sown together there is no prohibition against eating them. And they joined additional doubts (Mabit 3:127; Maharit Tzahalon, Ḥadashot 31; Maharashdam; Knesset Ha-gedola; Birkei Yosef 296:1). And in my humble opinion, there is room to say that all their leniency was when the markets were intended mainly for gentiles, since they were the majority; but today, if it is known that there are gentiles who grow kil'ayim in order to sell them in a market intended mainly for Jewish buyers, perhaps the kil'ayim have the status of "kavua" (fixed), which is not nullified by the majority. And although one may be lenient when it became mixed in randomly, if they regularly sell kil'ayim produce in certain places, it is forbidden to buy produce from there as long as there is a doubt whether it is kil'ayim. And certainly kashrut organizations that strive for hiddur (enhanced observance) must be careful about this.

sections.body_en:
The prohibition of kil'ayim of the vineyard is unique of its kind, for in addition to its being forbidden to mix grain and vegetables with a vine, what grows from this mixture is forbidden to be eaten and for benefit, as it is stated (Devarim 22:9): "You shall not sow your vineyard with kil'ayim, lest the full produce of the seed that you sow and the yield of the vineyard become consecrated (tikdash)." "Kadosh" means designated and set aside for a special purpose. Usually the meaning is something positive and elevated, but there are those who dedicate themselves to sin, like a harlot, who is called "kedesha" (Bereshit 38:21). Likewise, the produce of kil'ayim of the vineyard, which has been designated for sin, has become consecrated to impurity and forbidden to all of Israel.

One can say that the severe prohibition of kil'ayim was established with respect to the vineyard because of the great power of wine for good and for bad. On the one hand, song and blessing are recited over wine, and on the other hand, wine can debase a person and cast him down into the depths of sin. Therefore a special mitzva of nezirut was established in relation to wine, so that those who feared that wine might incline their heart toward evil, or prevent them from ascending the levels of holiness, would vow abstinence from wine; and an entire tractate of the Talmud, tractate Nazir, was even devoted to this. Since wine can sway a person's mind, the Torah warned the kohanim not to drink wine while performing their service, and likewise it is forbidden for a person who has drunk wine to pray (Peninei Halakha, Tefila 5:11). Likewise, the Torah was more stringent regarding kil'ayim of the vineyard than regarding the other prohibitions of kil'ayim, so that we would be extra careful in everything relating to wine, so that drinking it would be done for the sake of the joy of a mitzva and not for the sake of letting loose and casting off responsibility (see Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 7:1-2).

One can further explain that grain, legumes and vegetables are essential for a person's existence; and although eating them involves no excessive craving, without them a person cannot survive. Therefore one must engage in the work of growing them with extra diligence and eat them regularly. In contrast, wine is not essential for a person's existence, but drinking it brings great joy, and it is intended for the joy of a mitzva. Blurring the boundaries between them is dangerous, because a person who relates to wine as to grain will drink it regularly, until he becomes addicted to his craving and turns into an alcoholic. And even if he does not become addicted, if he drinks a great deal of it every day, wine will lose its special role in the joy of a mitzva. And on the other hand, a person who relates to grain as to the vine, as something not essential for his existence, will become lazy, and thorns will grow in his field instead of grain (see Shemen Ra'anan p. 333, from our master Rav Kook, of blessed memory).
